CHAPTER 01 · TEXT & PAPER ROUTE

Start with a good question.

Equivalent reading and exercises for working without the interactive app. Use paper or a local document. No software installation, account creation or market data is required. Suggested study time is 180 minutes, including feedback and correction; this estimate has not been validated by a learner pilot.

This is formative self-study. No answer is sent to a teacher. Record your attempts and corrections honestly; completion is a learning record, not a credential. The browser route has the same core tasks and a local progress export. This paper route does not automatically update that progress.

1. Set up your workspace · 15 minutes

Choose paper or a local document for your answers. A calculator is allowed. Write the chapter title and date. Create headings for your starting-point answers, instruments, worked case, experiment log, independent check, research card and corrections. Avoid recording personal financial details.

You can print this page using your browser. It contains the lesson, task prompts, formative explanations and a self-check answer section. The interactive version offers automatic feedback; this route requires you to compare your own work after attempting the tasks.

Completion requires: an ungraded diagnostic; four correct instrument classifications after correction; a completed stress calculation; a non-benchmark allocation tested in both scenarios with one hand calculation; at least 5/6 on the independent check including questions 3 and 6; and a research card with one specific revision. There is no time limit.

2. Check your starting point · 30 minutes

  1. £100 becomes £110. Calculate the percentage increase.
  2. Half of a portfolio earns 4%, and half earns 0%. Calculate its overall return.
  3. Which evidence can measure a price change: two dated prices; the highest price only; or an unlabeled upward line?

Record confidence as unsure, somewhat confident or confident. Confidence is ungraded.

Feedback after trying

1. The increase is 10%: (110 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100. The gain is £10; the percentage has no pound unit. 2. The portfolio earns 2%: 0.5 × 4% + 0.5 × 0%. 3. You need both dated prices. A maximum or an unlabeled line is insufficient.

Bridge or extension

If you missed an item, work through this bridge. A percentage change equals (ending value − starting value) ÷ starting value × 100. A weight is the fraction of a portfolio in an investment. Multiply each holding's return by its weight and add the contributions. Try £400 becoming £420, then explain your denominator.

If you answered all three correctly, calculate the percentage fall from £100 to £80 and the subsequent percentage rise back to £100. Explain why adding those changes misrepresents the round trip.

Compare your workings

The bridge answer is 5%. The extension is a 20% fall followed by a 25% rise. The starting base changes; the final compound return is 0%, because the investment returns to its original value. Write a correction if needed.

3. Meet the instruments · 35 minutes

Cash deposit: a balance held at a bank under account terms. Interest, access, bank risk and deposit protection depend on the account and jurisdiction. Inflation can reduce purchasing power.

Bond: a debt claim on an issuer, usually involving promised interest and repayment. The promise is subject to default risk. A bond's market price may fall before maturity, including when interest rates rise.

Share: a part ownership stake in a company. Neither dividends nor a positive resale outcome is guaranteed.

Fund / ETF: an interest in a pooled vehicle holding investments. An ETF trades on an exchange. Risk depends on its holdings, fees, concentration and structure. A fund label alone does not establish diversification.

A market is a mechanism for exchanging claims. A price records what traders are willing to transact at a point in time; it does not promise a future price.

Worked distinction

A bond fund is not a single bond. A bond may promise repayment on a date, subject to default. A fund may continuously replace its holdings; its units generally have no equivalent fixed repayment value on your chosen date. Look through the wrapper to the claim and the exposure.

Predict: would three funds necessarily diversify more than one? Explain what information you need before reading further.

Prediction feedback

Inspect underlying holdings and common exposures. Several funds can hold the same companies or share sector risks. The number of labels does not establish diversification.

Classify and correct

  1. A balance in a bank account.
  2. A company promises interest and repayment at maturity.
  3. Part ownership of one listed company.
  4. A listed vehicle holding a basket of investments.
Classification feedback

1. Cash deposit. 2. Bond. 3. Share. 4. Fund / ETF. If you missed one, state whether the claim involves a bank balance, lending, ownership or pooled holdings, then correct it. All four should be correct after revision.

Transfer: a friend says, “My technology ETF owns 30 businesses, so it cannot lose much.” Write two sentences distinguishing the vehicle from its holdings and identifying a shared risk. Self-check: explain pooled ownership, technology-sector concentration and the possibility of losses. Avoid promising a specific degree of protection.

4. Complete a worked case · 25 minutes

Maya compares a 50% cash / 40% bond / 10% share allocation with a fixed 20% cash / 40% bond / 40% share baseline. Both start at £1,000, buy at the start, and hold for one year without rebalancing. Fees, taxes and trading costs are zero for this first illustration. These are invented assets and returns, not observations or forecasts.

Supplied one-year scenario returns
AssetSteadyStress
Cash+2%+1%
Bonds+3%−5%
Shares+8%−20%

In the steady case, baseline return = 0.20 × 2 + 0.40 × 3 + 0.40 × 8 = 4.8%. It ends at £1,048. Maya's return is 0.50 × 2 + 0.40 × 3 + 0.10 × 8 = 3.0%, ending at £1,030. The difference is 1.8 percentage points, or £18 on this starting value.

Predict which allocation loses less under stress and explain why. Then calculate both stress returns, both ending values and the positive percentage-point gap between their losses.

Worked-case feedback

The baseline returns −9.8% and ends at £902. Maya's allocation returns −3.5% and ends at £965. The gap is 6.3 percentage points or £63. Maya gives up return in the steady scenario in exchange for smaller losses in this stress scenario. That is a scenario trade-off, not proof that her allocation is superior or suitable for a person.

A benchmark is a declared baseline. Use the same observation period and declared cost conventions. Choose the comparator because it fits the question, before seeing which result looks flattering. When deliberately comparing different asset exposures, as here, the risk difference is part of the question. When evaluating a strategy on a given exposure, use a matching baseline.

A useful question states a rule, comparator, observation period and measurable criterion. “What is best?” leaves these hidden. “Does this rule reduce maximum drawdown against its matching baseline over the supplied period after declared costs?” specifies evidence. Maximum drawdown is the largest fall from an earlier portfolio-value peak; calculation comes in a later chapter.

5. Run the paper allocation lab · 35 minutes

Use the table above and the same £1,000 starting value, zero-cost assumptions and one-year holding period. Choose your own non-benchmark weights from 0 to 100, adding to 100%.

  1. Predict the effect relative to 20 / 40 / 40 and record your confidence.
  2. Calculate return in the steady scenario: (cash weight ÷ 100 × 2) + (bond weight ÷ 100 × 3) + (share weight ÷ 100 × 8).
  3. Calculate return in the stress scenario using 1, −5 and −20 respectively, keeping the same allocation.
  4. Convert each return to ending value: £1,000 × (1 + return ÷ 100).
  5. Record weights, scenario, return, ending value and difference from the baseline for every attempt. Keep unfavourable results too.
  6. Check one ending value independently by calculating the pound change of each holding and adding it to £1,000.
  7. Explain the trade-off, revise the prediction if needed and name one model limitation.
Example for self-check

A 60% cash / 30% bond / 10% share allocation returns 2.9% in steady conditions, ending at £1,029, and −2.9% in stress, ending at £971. The baseline earns 4.8% and −9.8%, so the differences are −1.9 and +6.9 percentage points. Real costs, different returns or within-year trading could alter the result.

Your chosen allocation may differ. Use the weighted contribution method to check it. Nothing in the exercise identifies an optimal allocation. Only two invented outcomes are supplied; no claim about real-world performance follows.

6. Independent check · 25 minutes

Attempt all six before opening feedback. You need five correct, including questions 3 and 6. Record the first answer, then any correction and why it changed. You can revisit lessons; there is no time limit.

  1. A city issues a security promising interest and repayment in five years. Is this a share, bond or cash deposit?
  2. A fund holds only three airline companies. Does it eliminate risk, possibly remain concentrated in one sector, or guarantee diversification?
  3. A rule uses 20% cash / 80% shares over one year. Choose its fairest baseline: matching buy-and-hold exposure with the same dates and cost conventions; bonds from a different year; or whichever index makes the rule look best.
  4. Choose the testable question: “Which strategy is best?”; “Will shares always rise?”; or “Over the supplied 12 months, does rule A have a smaller maximum drawdown than its matching baseline after the same declared costs?”
  5. Half of a £1,000 portfolio earns 6% and half earns 0%. Does it end at £1,060, £1,030 or £1,003?
  6. A synthetic scenario favours a rule. Does this guarantee real profits, support only a conditional conclusion about that scenario, or prove the question was well designed?
Independent-check feedback: open after attempting
  1. Bond. It is a debt claim, subject to the issuer's ability to pay.
  2. It may remain concentrated in one sector. Inspect holdings and shared risks.
  3. Matching buy-and-hold exposure, dates and cost conventions. A comparator chosen to flatter the outcome is not fair.
  4. The third question states a rule, comparator, period and measurable criterion.
  5. £1,030: 0.5 × 6% + 0.5 × 0% = 3%.
  6. Only the conditional conclusion is justified. Invented scenarios illustrate assumptions, not real market performance.

If you miss the pass criteria, correct the misconception and try a changed case: use a 40% cash / 60% bond matching baseline and calculate 40% earning 5%, 60% earning 0% on £1,000. The numerical result should be £1,020. Record what changed in your reasoning. Passing after correction is valid formative completion.

7. Write your research card · 15 minutes

Write four short sections: (1) your exact allocation and holding rule; (2) the baseline and why it fits; (3) the scenarios, starting value, costs and measurable comparison; (4) a limitation and a result that would weaken your claim.

Then self-check: can someone reproduce the rule; are comparison assumptions stated consistently; will unfavourable results be reported; is the conclusion limited to the evidence? Make one specific revision and explain why it improves testability.

Exemplar for comparison after drafting

“I will compare buy-and-hold 50 / 40 / 10 with the fixed 20 / 40 / 40 baseline, starting each at £1,000 in both invented one-year scenarios. I will report total returns and percentage-point differences. I expect smaller stress losses but lower steady returns. Real costs or different returns could change the result. These scenarios do not establish future performance.”

A complete card states the rule, baseline, observations, criterion and limits. Its quality is self-reviewed, not established by a length check. Retain your workings, attempt history and revision as your chapter record. No instructor response is required.
